props.title: Raging Sharks
props.initialSlug: Killer sharks terrorize underwater research station

sections.content: Raging Sharks represents the bottom-tier of shark exploitation films, making even Shark Attack 3: Megalodon (2002) look sophisticated. It's a perfect example of mid-2000s direct-to-video creature features that tried capitalizing on the success of Deep Blue Sea (1999) but lacked the budget, effects, or coherent storytelling. The film's premise about alien crystals causing sharks to attack feels like someone threw darts at a board of B-movie plot elements.

sections.content: The early-to-mid 2000s saw an explosion of cheap shark movies trying to ride the wave of Shark Attack (1999) and Deep Blue Sea (1999). Studios like Nu Image and The Asylum churned out titles like Shark Zone (2003) and Shark Hunter (2001) with minimal budgets and maximum cheese. The CGI was typically atrocious, using the same stock footage of real sharks awkwardly inserted into scenes.

What's fascinating about Raging Sharks is how it exemplifies the weird sci-fi hybrid trend that tried making shark movies "fresh." Films like Sharks in Venice (2008) and Shark in Venice (2008) - yes, two different movies - attempted similar genre mashups. The results were usually incoherent messes that satisfied neither horror nor sci-fi fans. SUBHEAD: The Rise of Sharksploitation

movies.title: Open Water
movies.slug: Based on true events, stranded scuba divers face sharks. Raw, realistic approach to shark terror

sections.content: While Jaws (1975) launched the killer shark genre with artistic legitimacy, the 2000s marked a decisive shift toward intentionally campy shark films. This eventually led to self-aware titles like Sharknado (2013) and Ghost Shark (2013). Raging Sharks sits awkwardly between serious attempt and accidental comedy, making it less entertaining than either approach.
